wiki_article:
**from The Crimson Hexagon — Origin Text** is a record **WITHHELD** as a confirmed wrong-object mismatch.

The record's title claims a primary creative text — the Origin Text of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive. **Its seated body is "The Provenance of Jack Feist," a provenance resolution document**, the same work held at **#111**; the body opens *"This document resolves the provenance of Jack Feist… performed against the primary archaeological stratum."*

Because the body genuinely *is* the provenance document, the duplicate-witness pointer to #111 is internally consistent — which is why the page read as a primary work superseded by its own analysis. **The pointer was never the defect; the body was.** The mismatch was corroborated by two independent instruments: the content-fingerprint scan paired #111 with #1193 at **0.80 content overlap against 0.42 title overlap**, and the SUBJECT detector flagged it on title-token coverage. **The Origin Text is displaced and not seated under this record.** Withheld 2026-08-05, disposition P0.

modifications.now: This document resolves the provenance of Jack Feist, literary heteronym and constituent voice of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive. The resolution is performed against the primary archaeological stratum: the Blogspot deposit dated March 14, 2015, titled "The Crimson Hexagon," included in _Pearl and Other Poems_ (ISBN-10: 0692313079). Jack Feist has been the longest-running unresolved entity in the archive's heteronymic registry, leaving the Space Ark Room in provisional status. This document closes the loop by anchoring Feist to specific material, digital, intertextual, and knowledge-graph coordinates -- and by demonstrating that the 2015 origin text contains, in embryonic literary form, the entire theoretical architecture the subsequent decade would formalize. The full text of the 2015 origin story is embedded in this document as a holographic kernel: the provenance document contains the creative work, and the creative work structurally anticipates the provenance document. "Prophecy" is used here in the archive's literary-historical sense: not supernatural prediction, but the earlier text's structurally exact anticipation of an architecture, conflict, and fulfillment whose full meaning becomes legible only later.[^1]. — Description restored 2026-08-05 from composed from the work's own opening prose; it replaces a batch-restoration stub that described the recovery event rather than the work. A fuller editorial treatment belongs to the description/wiki review stream.
